questions.question: In Computer Networks, what is a primary characteristic of a "Client-Server" network architecture?
questions.title: Client-Server architecture — primary characteristic
options: A central server provides services and clients request them
Clients provide the resources to the server
Every node is both client and server
questions.answer: A central server provides services and clients request them

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A dedicated, centralized **server provides resources/services, while multiple clients request and consume those services** — the server typically has higher resources/uptime, and all client requests are routed through it (centralized control, unlike P2P's decentralization).

questions.question: In Computer Networks, what is the term for the time it takes for a packet to travel from source to destination and back again?
questions.title: Time for a packet to travel to destination and back

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This is called **Round Trip Time (RTT)**.

questions.question: In Computer Networks, what does the acronym "CIDR" stand for?
questions.title: CIDR acronym

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Classless Inter-Domain Routing** — a method for allocating IP addresses and routing using variable-length subnet masking instead of fixed classful boundaries.

questions.question: In Computer Networks, which wireless security protocol provides the highest level of encryption among the choices?
questions.title: Wireless security protocol with highest encryption

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **WPA3** (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) provides the strongest encryption among current standards (WEP < WPA < WPA2 < WPA3), using stronger cryptographic protocols (SAE instead of PSK) and forward secrecy.

questions.question: In Computer Networks, which layer of the OSI model provides services to applications?
questions.title: OSI layer providing services to applications

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The **Application Layer (Layer 7)** provides network services directly to end-user applications (e.g., HTTP, FTP, SMTP).

questions.question: In Computer Networks, what does the term "Payload" refer to?
questions.title: "Payload" term
options: The actual data carried inside a packet, excluding headers
questions.answer: The actual data carried inside a packet, excluding headers

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Payload refers to **the actual data being carried/transmitted within a packet or frame**, excluding the header and control/overhead information added for routing and protocol management.

questions.question: In Computer Networks, which protocol is responsible for managing multicast group memberships?
questions.title: Protocol managing multicast group memberships

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol)** manages multicast group membership between hosts and routers on a local network.

questions.question: Which distance-vector routing protocol mechanism prevents routing loops by ensuring a router never advertises a route back onto the exact interface from which it was originally learned?
questions.title: Distance-vector loop prevention — never advertise back on same interface

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This mechanism is called **Split Horizon** — a router refrains from advertising a route back out of the same interface through which it originally learned that route, preventing simple two-node routing loops.

questions.question: In Computer Networks, what is the primary function of an Intrusion Detection System (IDS)?
questions.title: Primary function of an IDS
options: Monitor traffic for suspicious activity and raise alerts
questions.answer: Monitor traffic for suspicious activity and raise alerts

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: An Intrusion Detection System **monitors network/system traffic for suspicious activity or known attack signatures and generates alerts** — unlike an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System), a pure IDS is passive/detective and does not actively block traffic.

questions.question: In Computer Networks, what is the purpose of an Ephemeral Port?
questions.title: Purpose of an Ephemeral Port
options: A port used only by DNS
A fixed port reserved for a well-known service
A temporary port assigned dynamically to a client for one connection
A port reserved by the kernel
questions.answer: A temporary port assigned dynamically to a client for one connection

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: An ephemeral port is a **short-lived, dynamically assigned port number (typically in the high range, e.g., 49152–65535) used temporarily by a client application as the source port for an outgoing connection**, released once the connection ends.

questions.question: What is the total bit size of a standard IPv6 address?
questions.title: IPv6 address bit size

questions.question: In the IPsec protocol suite, what is the primary operational difference between the Authentication Header (AH) protocol and the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)?
questions.title: IPsec — AH vs ESP
options: AH works at the application layer; ESP at the physical layer
AH encrypts data; ESP only authenticates
AH gives authentication and integrity only; ESP also provides encryption
questions.answer: AH gives authentication and integrity only; ESP also provides encryption

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **AH (Authentication Header)** provides **authentication and data integrity only** (no encryption/confidentiality) for the entire packet including parts of the IP header. **ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload)** provides **encryption (confidentiality) in addition to authentication and integrity**, but typically doesn't cover the outer IP header — ESP is far more commonly used because it protects payload confidentiality.

questions.question: In Computer Networks, what is the purpose of a network interface card (NIC)?
questions.title: Purpose of a NIC (Network Interface Card)
options: Connect a computer to a network
questions.answer: Connect a computer to a network

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A NIC **provides the physical/hardware interface that connects a computer to a network**, handling the conversion between the computer's internal data and the electrical/optical/radio signals used on the network medium, and it has a unique MAC address for identification.

questions.question: Which application layer protocol relies entirely on UDP port 69 and provides a simplistic, unauthenticated mechanism for transferring small configuration files to network devices?
questions.title: Application protocol on UDP port 69, unauthenticated file transfer

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol)** — a simplified, connectionless, unauthenticated file transfer protocol commonly used to push configuration files to network devices.

questions.question: In Computer Networks, what is the main function of the CSMA/CA protocol?
questions.title: Main function of CSMA/CA
options: Avoid collisions in wireless networks by sensing the channel and backing off
Detect collisions on wired Ethernet after they occur
Assign IP addresses to wireless clients
questions.answer: Avoid collisions in wireless networks by sensing the channel and backing off

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision **Avoidance**) is used mainly in wireless networks to **listen for a clear channel before transmitting and use techniques (like random backoff and RTS/CTS handshaking) to avoid/minimize collisions**, since wireless devices can't reliably detect collisions while transmitting (unlike wired CSMA/CD).

questions.question: Which standard port is used by the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) to allow users to connect to another computer over a network connection?
questions.title: Standard port used by RDP

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **TCP port 3389**.

questions.question: Which routing protocol utilizes Dijkstra's Shortest Path First algorithm to construct a loop-free topological map of the entire autonomous system?
questions.title: Routing protocol using Dijkstra's SPF algorithm

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)** — a link-state routing protocol that uses Dijkstra's algorithm to build a complete, loop-free shortest-path topology map of the entire autonomous system.

questions.question: In the standard IPv6 packet header, which field replaces the IPv4 "Time to Live" (TTL) field while serving the exact same routing loop-prevention purpose?
questions.title: IPv6 field replacing IPv4's TTL

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The **Hop Limit** field in the IPv6 header serves the exact same purpose as IPv4's TTL — it's decremented at each router hop, and the packet is discarded when it reaches zero, preventing infinite routing loops.

questions.question: During the standard TCP three-way handshake connection establishment, what is the mathematically correct sequence of control flags exchanged between the client and the server?
questions.title: TCP three-way handshake — flag sequence

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The sequence is: **Client sends SYN → Server responds with SYN-ACK → Client responds with ACK** (often written as SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK), after which the connection is established.

questions.question: Which IEEE networking standard explicitly defines the frame tagging mechanism used to logically separate broadcast domains across a physical switch infrastructure using VLANs?
questions.title: IEEE standard for VLAN frame tagging

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **IEEE 802.1Q** defines the standard mechanism for VLAN tagging on Ethernet frames, allowing multiple logical broadcast domains to coexist on a shared physical switch infrastructure.

questions.question: Given an IP address of 192.168.1.130 with a subnet mask of /27, what is the valid range of assignable host addresses for this specific subnetwork?
questions.title: Subnetting: 192.168.1.130 /27 — valid host range

sections.label: Steps
sections.content:
1. /27 means the subnet mask is 255.255.255.224, leaving 5 host bits → block size = 2⁵ = 32.
2. Subnet boundaries in the last octet go: 0, 32, 64, 96, 128, 160, 192, 224...
3. .130 falls between 128 and 160, so this subnet's network address is **192.168.1.128** and broadcast address is **192.168.1.159** (128 + 32 − 1).
4. Valid assignable host addresses exclude the network and broadcast addresses.

questions.question: In Computer Networks, what happens when an IP packet's TTL (Time to Live) reaches zero?
questions.title: What happens when a packet's TTL reaches zero
options: The packet is forwarded to the default gateway
The packet is delivered to the destination
The router discards the packet and sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message
questions.answer: The router discards the packet and sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The router that decrements the TTL to zero **discards (drops) the packet** and typically sends an ICMP "Time Exceeded" message back to the source — this prevents packets from circulating indefinitely due to routing loops.

questions.question: Which specific type of Network Address Translation allows multiple internal private IP addresses to simultaneously share a single public IP address by utilizing distinct port numbers?
questions.title: NAT type allowing multiple private IPs to share one public IP via ports

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **PAT (Port Address Translation)**, also known as **NAT Overload** — it maps multiple internal private IP addresses to a single public IP address, distinguishing the separate sessions using different source port numbers.

questions.question: What is the total bit size of a standard IPv4 address?
questions.title: IPv4 address bit size

questions.question: In Computer Networks, what does the term "packet loss" refer to?
questions.title: "Packet loss" term
options: Transmitted packets that never reach their destination
questions.answer: Transmitted packets that never reach their destination

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Packet loss refers to **one or more transmitted packets failing to reach their destination** (dropped due to network congestion, errors, faulty hardware, etc.), typically measured as a percentage of packets sent versus received.

questions.question: In Computer Networks, which DNS record type is used to map a domain name to an IPv6 address?
questions.title: DNS record type mapping domain to IPv6 address

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The **AAAA record** (as opposed to the A record, which maps to an IPv4 address).

questions.question: What is the term for a network of private computers infected with malicious software and controlled as a group without the owners' knowledge?
questions.title: Network of infected computers controlled as a group

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This is called a **Botnet** — a collection of malware-infected devices ("bots" or "zombies") remotely controlled by an attacker, typically without the owners' knowledge, often used for DDoS attacks, spam, or data theft.

questions.question: In Computer Networks, what is a primary characteristic of a "Peer-to-Peer" (P2P) network architecture?
questions.title: Peer-to-Peer (P2P) architecture — primary characteristic
options: A single dedicated server serves all nodes
Nodes can act only as clients
A central router controls all data
Every node can act as both client and server
questions.answer: Every node can act as both client and server

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: In P2P, **every node (peer) can act as both a client and a server**, sharing resources directly with other peers without relying on a centralized dedicated server — control and resources are decentralized across all participants.

questions.question: In Computer Networks, what does the acronym "IPsec" stand for?
questions.title: IPsec acronym

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Internet Protocol Security** — a suite of protocols that secures IP communications through authentication and encryption of each IP packet in a data stream.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of TCP over UDP?
questions.title: What is the main advantage of TCP over UDP?
options: TCP guarantees reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery via acknowledgments and retransmission
TCP has lower latency than UDP in all cases
TCP does not require a connection to be established
UDP cannot be used for real-time applications
questions.answer: TCP guarantees reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery via acknowledgments and retransmission

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: TCP and UDP are the two primary transport-layer protocols, trading off reliability against speed/overhead.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **TCP provides reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery** through mechanisms like sequence numbers, acknowledgments, and retransmission of lost packets — at the cost of higher overhead/latency compared to UDP, which is connectionless and provides no delivery guarantees (used where speed matters more than reliability, e.g., video streaming, DNS).

questions.question: What does DNS (Domain Name System) primarily do?
questions.title: What does DNS (Domain Name System) primarily do?
options: Translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses
Encrypts traffic between client and server
Assigns IP addresses dynamically to devices on a network
Routes packets along the shortest path
questions.answer: Translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: DNS operates as a distributed, hierarchical naming system across the internet.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **DNS translates human-friendly domain names (like example.com) into the numeric IP addresses computers actually use to route traffic**, functioning like the internet's phone book (DHCP handles dynamic IP assignment, which is a different protocol).

questions.question: What is the purpose of a firewall in network security?
questions.title: What is the purpose of a firewall in network security?
options: To monitor and control incoming/outgoing traffic based on predefined security rules
To physically prevent cable damage in a data center
To translate domain names into IP addresses
questions.answer: To monitor and control incoming/outgoing traffic based on predefined security rules

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Firewalls act as a barrier between trusted internal networks and untrusted external networks.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **A firewall monitors and filters incoming and outgoing network traffic based on a defined set of security rules**, blocking or allowing traffic to protect the network from unauthorized access and threats.
